programme: PML and HIPK2 form the PML-nuclear-body/HIPK2 apoptotic checkpoint: HIPK2 is itself a transcriptional target of PML, and the two factors converge on the same downstream nodes (TP53, CDKN1A) among their target sets, consistent with the documented biology in which SUMO-dependent HIPK2 recruitment to PML-NBs licenses p53 Ser46 phosphorylation and a DNA-damage/apoptotic response.
role_in_a: In AML this checkpoint is disabled rather than active: the PML-RARA fusion that defines acute promyelocytic leukemia (a major AML subtype) disrupts normal PML-NB assembly, and HIPK2 itself carries a functional impairment of its SUMO-interacting motif in AML — the same motif needed for PML-NB recruitment — removing the brake that would otherwise force damaged blasts into apoptosis and permitting differentiation block and blast survival.
role_in_b: In ischemic stroke, HIPK2 is induced in neurons after injury and drives a pro-apoptotic/pro-injury programme (documented here via an HIPK2-HDAC3 axis causing mitochondrial fragmentation), i.e. the same factor operating as an active death signal in post-ischemic tissue rather than as a suppressed checkpoint.
shared_axis: Both diseases turn on the same PML/HIPK2-anchored p53 checkpoint (TP53 and CDKN1A sit among both factors' targets), but with opposite valence: AML survives by disabling it (fused PML, SUMO-motif-impaired HIPK2), while stroke tissue is damaged by its activation (HIPK2 induction after ischemia) — a checkpoint reused for opposite ends in a proliferative versus a degenerative disease.
reasoning: Each disease is separately and directly documented for a component of this axis — PML-RARA/APL and HIPK2-SIM impairment in AML, HIPK2 induction in post-stroke neurons — and the target-overlap (TP53, CDKN1A) plus HIPK2 being a literal PML target argues the module is real and not coincidental. But no retrieved paper documents PML acting through this axis in stroke specifically, and the stroke HIPK2 paper implicates a different partner (HDAC3, not PML/p53), so the cross-disease link rests on generalizing from AML-side evidence rather than on retrieved joint evidence.
support: PMID 30755814 — HIPK2's SUMO-interacting motif is functionally impaired in AML, the same motif required for PML-NB recruitment, directly tying HIPK2 dysfunction to the PML axis in this disease. PMID 42524167 and PMID 42133174 — place PML (as PML-RARA) in acute promyelocytic leukemia, an AML subtype. PMID 39079624 — places HIPK2 in stroke via an HDAC3/mitochondrial-fragmentation axis, independent evidence for HIPK2 in neuronal injury but not via PML. No PMID above documents PML in stroke: the retrieved 'PML' stroke papers concern progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, an unrelated demyelinating disease sharing the acronym, and are not evidence for this axis.
how_to_falsify: In an ischemic-stroke neuronal model, knock down PML and test whether HIPK2-dependent p53 Ser46 phosphorylation and apoptosis are affected. If HIPK2's pro-apoptotic activity in post-ischemic neurons is unchanged by PML loss (i.e., it runs entirely through HDAC3 or another route independent of PML-NBs), that would show the AML-side PML-HIPK2 partnership does not extend to the stroke context and the account is wrong.
caveats: 27 patient-group comparisons across only 4 independent cohort pairs is a modest base, and both carrying factors recur at the lower end of the concordant list (PML 14/27, HIPK2 11/27) rather than at the top (HOXA11 19/27, MAML1 16/27), which were left out because their targets do not converge on this checkpoint. Open Targets itself is consistent with the caveat above: PML scores near baseline for stroke (percentile 0.197) despite scoring almost maximally for AML (0.989), matching the finding that the retrieved 'PML-stroke' literature is a name collision (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy) rather than genuine association. None of the tissue-generic exclusions (STAT5A, LEF1, IRF1, ERG, STAT1, NFATC1, FOXO4, GFI1, SMAD3, E2F3, ID3, EBF1 — all myeloid/immune-generic) overlap this module, so its presence is not an artifact of failing to strip a blood-generic regulator.
